I've been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when they rolled out the T-Mobile ONE plan. I've been getting a military discount the entire time, but even with that, plus T-Mobile's many price hikes, my monthly bill has slowly climbed to $113. I've had enough, and I've started looking for cheaper options. Couple that with the fact that the iPhone 18 Pro costs at least $100 more this year, so saving money on my phone bill helps offset the cost of upgrading. That's why I started looking into MVNOs.

What is an MVNO?

MVNO stands for "Mobile Virtual Network Operator." Simply put, an MVNO is a wireless service provider that doesn't own its own nationwide cellular network. They don't build their own network; instead, they buy capacity from the major carriers like AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, and resell it to their customers. Think of them as "middlemen" for wireless service.

Choosing an MVNO doesn't necessarily mean giving up the network you're currently using. Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile's network, Visible uses Verizon's network, and US Mobile lets customers choose between all three major networks. This article focuses on those three MVNOs because they are the ones I researched most thoroughly before leaving T-Mobile, but there are plenty of other options out there.

At the end of the day, an MVNO is just a way to buy wireless service without going through the network operator directly.

Why are MVNOs cheaper? What are the drawbacks?

If an MVNO uses the exact same network as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how can they charge so much less? The short answer is that MVNOs don't incur all the costs of running a nationwide wireless operation. They don't have to build or maintain a network, many of them operate primarily online rather than maintaining physical stores, and they have fewer employees. The savings are passed on to customers in the form of lower monthly rates.

MVNO plans also tend to be simpler, without the "perks" and extras that big carriers offer. Depending on the carrier and plan, you might not get free streaming services or other perks that keep you with a major carrier. But if you really want those "free" services, the money you save with an MVNO will often be enough to pay for those subscriptions yourself.

That's exactly my situation. I used to love the free MLB.TV subscription that came with T-Mobile, and I used it every season; but I never watch Netflix, so the "free Netflix" perk does absolutely nothing for me. Even if I wanted both Netflix and MLB.TV, I could subscribe to both myself and still come out ahead by switching to an MVNO. For me, the important thing is having reliable, affordable wireless service—I don't need the extras that T-Mobile offers.

The "drawbacks" aren't so much that the service is worse, but that you pay less and get less. What exactly you give up depends on which MVNO and which plan you choose. Video streaming might be limited to lower resolutions, the amount of high-speed or prioritized data might vary, and network priority might be different. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, and I rarely go to concerts or sporting events where the crowds can bog down the network, so network priority doesn't make much of a difference in my daily use. But I do travel internationally occasionally, so international data is an important consideration for me. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, while others charge extra or offer limited coverage.

There are also some less obvious differences, especially if you want to buy a new iPhone. If your carrier is an MVNO, you won't have access to Apple Card monthly installments or the iPhone Upgrade Program. Those options are limited to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. Practically speaking, if you buy your iPhone directly from Apple, you typically have to pay for it up front. The big carriers also offer significant trade-in deals and promotions that MVNOs generally can't match. Not all MVNOs support Apple Watch, so if you use a cellular model, be sure to check first.

Finally, most MVNOs offer support primarily by phone and online rather than having staff at a retail store who can help you troubleshoot problems in person. I consider myself fairly tech-savvy, and I don't want to make a special trip to a store for minor issues. In my experience, the people in the store end up calling the same support line anyway, and the wait times are just as long, so this is a complete non-issue for me.

The point is, these limitations don't apply to every MVNO—it all depends on the carrier and the plan—so it's important to know exactly what you're getting before you switch.

Three MVNOs worth considering

After deciding to leave T-Mobile, I started keeping an eye on my options. Verizon and AT&T's postpaid plans were more expensive than what I was already paying, so the other two major carriers were out. I ultimately narrowed my search to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each had something that appealed to me, and all of them would allow me to significantly lower my monthly bill without giving up access to a major carrier's network.

US Mobile is arguably the most flexible of the three, and it's the carrier I ultimately switched to from T-Mobile. That doesn't mean it's right for you, or even that it's the best of the three. It's just the one that best fits my personal needs.

US Mobile wasn't actually my first choice—I had never even heard of the company before I started researching MVNOs. But the more I learned about it, the more it stood out. Here's why: US Mobile operates on all three major networks in the United States, letting customers choose the network that works best for them. It also offers a Multi-Network add-on that lets you activate two networks on the same iPhone (the add-on network's line runs in the background), so when your primary network signal is weak or has no coverage, your iPhone can automatically switch to the other network (US Mobile calls this switching when "coverage is lower"). You'll need to enable "Allow Cellular Data Switching" in your iPhone's Cellular settings for this to work. US Mobile charges extra for this add-on, which I personally don't need, but it's nice to have the option.

I had just moved and wanted to see how Verizon's coverage compared to T-Mobile's around our new home, so I decided to try both. I put my wife's iPhone on US Mobile's Light Speed network (i.e., T-Mobile) and mine on Warp (i.e., Verizon) to compare coverage head-to-head. In our area, Verizon was clearly better, so switching to US Mobile was a win-win: significantly lower monthly bill and better coverage.

Mint Mobile was actually my first choice because it's a T-Mobile sub-brand, meaning I'd be back on the network I'm familiar with, just for less money. What I didn't like is that it doesn't include international data. My wife and I enjoy cruises, and we travel abroad frequently, so being able to use cellular data when we travel is important to us. Mint does offer international data service, but it's an extra charge that quickly eats into some of the savings. I also wasn't a fan of taxes and surcharges being billed separately.

Visible is similarly straightforward, but it only uses Verizon's network. My biggest concern with Visible was Verizon's coverage in my area. After almost a decade with T-Mobile, I know exactly how its network performs, but I had no idea what kind of coverage Verizon had. That alone made me initially choose US Mobile over Visible, because US Mobile let me try Verizon while still having the option of switching to T-Mobile or AT&T. Visible's top unlimited data plan includes free Apple Watch cellular service, which is appealing. (US Mobile's Warp/Verizon network offers the same perk on its top plan.)

What you need to switch

Switching to an MVNO was easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones, and moving both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile took about 10 minutes, and I never left the couch. You'll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, although I'm focused on iPhones), and some information from your current carrier. If you want to keep your existing phone number, be sure not to cancel your current service until the number has fully transferred.

Here's what you'll need:

  • Your current carrier's account number
  • Port-out PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

I prepaid US Mobile for a year of unlimited data plans on two lines to prepare for the switch. My wife doesn't use Apple Watch cellular service and doesn't care about higher-quality video, so she went with US Mobile's Unlimited Starter plan, saving $100 over the Unlimited Premium plan I chose. Two lines plus an Apple Watch plan came to $500 for the year, compared to $1,356 my wife and I were paying T-Mobile for two lines without Apple Watch service. (Keep in mind, that price already includes my military discount.)

Getting the Port-out PIN from T-Mobile was straightforward. I expected the process to be hidden and complicated, but it wasn't. The steps for Verizon and AT&T are also listed below.

After connecting my iPhone to Wi-Fi, US Mobile immediately sent over the new eSIM, and the installation process was as simple as tapping a button in an email and following a few prompts. My wife's iPhone followed the same steps. The only additional step was setting up my Apple Watch, which I did easily through the US Mobile app.

Why I'll stick with an MVNO

Same coverage, lower bill: When I do the math on what I'm saving, the trade-offs I've made are absolutely worth it. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, so I don't use much cellular data (but based on speed test results, US Mobile is just as fast as T-Mobile). Most importantly, when I'm away from Wi-Fi, the cellular signal is still strong and reliable, especially for calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have actually done away with traditional contracts in favor of device installment plans, which is basically just another way to lock you into their network until you've paid off the device. I've always bought my iPhones directly from Apple because I value the freedom of owning an unlocked phone, but I'm also glad to see that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible all don't have contracts.

Easy to switch: Most MVNOs let you pay month-to-month, so you're not locked into a long-term contract. If one carrier has a great promotion this month, and another has an even better deal next month, you can switch quickly and easily. Prepaid accounts also don't require a credit check—which means switching won't leave a hard inquiry on your credit report dragging down your credit score, and you won't be turned away because of poor credit. My credit is in good shape, but even switching from T-Mobile to Verizon, I wouldn't want a hard inquiry on my record.

Top comment from Richard Lewis (Rich):

I switched from AT&T to Mint Mobile a few years ago. It was one of the smartest tech decisions I've ever made.

Prepaying for a year saves more: The tradeoff for that flexibility is that if you're willing to prepay for a year of service, you can save even more. Most MVNOs offer significant discounts on annual plans, so you have to weigh the freedom to switch at any time against a lower overall cost.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I enjoy taking cruises. If you've ever gotten on a ship and forgotten to turn on airplane mode, letting your iPhone automatically connect to the ship's network, you know just how shocking the bill can be. With a prepaid plan, you don't have to worry about accidentally racking up enormous roaming charges. Unless international roaming service is included, my phone simply won't connect to a foreign network and charge me. US Mobile plans also include taxes and fees, so what you see is what you pay.

Switching to an MVNO isn't about getting the cheapest service possible; it's about paying a fair price for the service you actually need, rather than paying for a bunch of stuff you'll never use. So far, I don't feel like I'm missing out on anything that's important to me (although I will miss that free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I now have an Apple Watch cellular line that I didn't have before, and my overall monthly bill is lower. My iPhone hasn't changed, my phone number hasn't changed, and the coverage I'm getting on US Mobile's Warp (Verizon) network is better than before—while still having the freedom to switch again whenever I want.

Your priorities may be different from mine, and MVNOs aren't for everyone. But if you're currently paying a lot for wireless service and you haven't considered an MVNO, it's worth a look. You might be surprised to find that there's actually very little you have to give up.
